title: How to get your business on Google Maps
desc: A step-by-step guide to setting up a free Google Business Profile, so your business shows on Google Maps and in local searches, even without a shop.
intro: When someone searches for a service “near me”, Google shows a map with three businesses before any websites. Those businesses all have one thing: a Google Business Profile. It’s free, and here’s how to set one up properly.
body:
What a Google Business Profile is

A Google Business Profile is the box that appears on Google Maps and in search results with your name, phone number, opening hours, photos and reviews. It’s free, and you manage it yourself. For a local business it’s often the first thing a customer sees, before they ever reach your website.

1. Start with the right Google account

Sign in to a Google account, ideally one using your business email, then go to business.google.com/create. Google’s own guide walks through each step: add or claim your Business Profile.

2. Check you don’t already have a listing

When you type your business name, Google may suggest an existing listing. If it’s yours, pick it and claim it rather than making a duplicate. If someone else has already verified it, Google lets you request ownership.

3. Choose your main category carefully

Your primary category tells Google what you are: “Painter”, “Hair salon”, “Wedding venue”. Pick the most specific one that fits, because it decides which searches you appear in.

4. No shop? You can hide your address

If customers don’t visit you (most tradespeople, cleaners, mobile hairdressers, caterers), set up as a service-area business. Google says you “should only choose to not show your address if your business is a service-area business”. You then list the towns or postcodes you cover; Google’s guide allows up to 20 and suggests staying within about two hours’ drive of your base.

5. Add your phone number and website

Use the number customers should actually call, and link your own website rather than a Facebook page if you have one. A website gives Google more to go on about what you do and where.

6. Verify it

Your profile only shows to customers once it’s verified. After you press Finish, Google offers the verification options available to you. Do it straight away rather than choosing “Verify later”.

7. Fill in everything, then keep it alive

Add opening hours, services, a description in plain English and plenty of real photos of your work. Then keep it current: update holiday hours, add new photos and reply to reviews.

8. Ask for reviews, the right way

Reviews help people choose you. Google lets you share a review link or QR code with customers (Google’s review tips). But never offer anything in return: Google treats rewarding reviews as fake engagement, which it says is “strictly prohibited”.

Your profile and your website work together

The profile gets you seen; your website is where people decide. Make sure your site loads fast on a phone, says clearly what you do and where, and makes it easy to call or get a quote. Our website checklist covers the rest. If you’d like help, our Business package includes help setting up your Google Business Profile.

title: How long does it take to build a small business website?
desc: What actually decides how long a website takes, what slows projects down, and the realistic timeline for a small business site, step by step.
intro: The honest answer is that the building is rarely the slow part. Most delays come from waiting for content and decisions. Here’s how a typical small business website project runs, and how to keep yours quick.
body:
The short answer

For a small business website of one to five pages, around two weeks is realistic once the designer has everything they need. Bigger sites with bookings, payments or lots of pages take longer, and a good designer will give you a timeline before you pay anything.

What happens in those two weeks

  • Talk: you explain what your business does, who your customers are and what the website needs to do.
  • Design: the designer shows you a first version early, so you can shape it.
  • Build: the site is built for phones first, with your text, photos, contact form and the pages Google needs.
  • Changes: you ask for changes. At NEMORA every package includes two rounds of changes before launch.
  • Launch: the site goes live on your domain.

What slows websites down

Content. Your logo, photos, prices, opening hours and the words about your business. If you have these ready on day one, projects fly.

Decisions. Long gaps between “here’s the draft” and your feedback add days or weeks. Set aside an hour to review properly.

Too many people. If several people need to approve every change, agree who has the final say before you start.

Domain access. If you already own a domain, find the login before you start. Hunting for an old account can hold up launch day.

How to get your site live faster

  • Send 10 to 20 of your best photos of real work, your premises or your team.
  • Write a few lines on what you do, where you work and why people choose you. The designer can polish it.
  • List your services and, if you’re happy to, your prices.
  • Look at two or three websites you like and say why.

Our timeline

At NEMORA, most sites go live within around two weeks once we have your content. Half the setup fee books your project and the rest is paid when your site is ready to go live. See our packages and prices, or read how much a website costs.

title: Do I need a website if I have a Facebook page?
desc: Facebook is useful, but it isn’t a website. What a Facebook page can’t do for your business, what a website adds, and when a page on its own is enough.
intro: Lots of small businesses start with a Facebook page, and plenty get work from it. So is a website worth paying for? Here’s an honest look at what each one does, and where a Facebook page falls short.
body:
What a Facebook page is good at

A Facebook page is free, quick to set up and great for staying in touch with people who already know you: posting new work, offers, events and updates. If your customers are mostly regulars and friends of friends, it does a lot.

Where a Facebook page falls short

People searching Google don’t find you. When someone who has never heard of you searches “electrician in Stoke” or “nail salon near me”, Google shows a map of Google Business Profiles and a list of websites. A Facebook page often isn’t what they find.

You don’t own it. Facebook decides how many people see your posts, what your page looks like and what you’re allowed to do. If your account is hacked or restricted, your shop window disappears overnight.

Not everyone uses Facebook. Some customers don’t have an account, and some won’t click into one to find your prices or opening hours.

It’s hard to look established. A page looks like everyone else’s page. A website with your own name, photos and domain makes a small business look like a proper business, which matters most for bigger jobs and business customers.

What a website adds

  • A place that shows up on Google for the services and towns you cover.
  • Your prices, services, areas and opening hours, laid out clearly in one place.
  • A contact or quote form that sends enquiries straight to you.
  • Your own domain and email address, which look more professional.
  • Something you control, however the social media apps change.

When a Facebook page alone is enough

If you’re fully booked from word of mouth, or you’re just testing an idea, a Facebook page and a free Google Business Profile may be all you need for now. When you want new customers who don’t already know you, a website is the next step.

The best answer: both

Use Facebook to stay in touch, and a website to be found and to look established. Link them together: your website on your Facebook page, and your Facebook on your website. Our checklist covers what your website needs, and our Starter package is a one-page website for £400, then £25 a month.

title: What should a small business website include?
desc: A plain-English checklist of what every small business website needs, from a clear headline and click-to-call to reviews, prices and a privacy notice.
intro: Most people decide whether to call you within a few seconds of landing on your website, usually on a phone. This checklist covers what needs to be there for them to pick up the phone instead of going back to Google.
body:
1. A headline that says what you do and where

Someone should know within five seconds what you do, who it’s for and where you work. “Painter and decorator in Wolverhampton” beats “Quality you can trust” every time, for visitors and for Google.

2. One obvious next step

Decide what you want a visitor to do (call, ask for a quote, book) and make that button the most visible thing on every page. Too many competing buttons means people choose none.

3. Click-to-call and a quick contact form

On a phone, your number should be one tap away. Keep forms short: name, contact details and a message is usually enough. Every extra field loses people.

4. Your services, clearly listed

List what you actually do, in the words your customers use. If you cover several services, give the main ones their own section or page so each can be found in search.

5. Prices, or at least a starting point

You don’t have to publish a full price list, but a “from” price or typical range saves time on both sides and filters out people who were never going to buy.

6. Real proof

Real photos of your work, reviews from real customers and the names of businesses you’ve worked with do more than any amount of clever copy. Stock photos and anonymous testimonials do the opposite.

7. Where you work

Say which towns and areas you cover. It reassures local customers and helps you appear in “near me” searches, especially alongside a Google Business Profile.

8. Fast and built for phones

Most visitors will see your site on a phone, often on mobile data. Pages should load quickly, text should be readable without zooming and buttons should be easy to tap.

9. The basics done properly

  • A page title and description for every page, so you look good in search results
  • A favicon and a preview image for when your link is shared
  • A secure (https) address
  • A privacy notice that explains what you do with people’s details, as UK GDPR requires
  • A way to update it yourself, or someone who will do it quickly

Want a second opinion on yours?

If you’re not sure how your current site measures up, send us the link and we’ll tell you honestly what we’d change. You can also see how we approach this in our recent work.

title: How much does a website cost for a small business?
desc: What a small business website costs in the UK, what affects the price, the hidden costs to ask about, and exactly what NEMORA charges.
intro: “How much is a website?” is a bit like “how much is a van?”. It depends what it needs to do. Here’s what actually drives the price, the costs that are easy to miss, and what we charge, so you can compare quotes properly.
body:
What affects the price

  • Number of pages. A one-page site costs less than a site with separate pages for each service, area and project.
  • Custom design or template. A design built around your brand takes longer than dropping your logo into a template, but it’s what makes you look different from everyone else.
  • Features. Quote forms, booking systems, member logins and card payments each add work. A booking or payment system is a different job from a brochure site.
  • Content. If you have your photos and wording ready, it’s quicker. If someone needs to write it for you, that’s extra time.
  • Who builds it. Doing it yourself on a website builder, hiring a freelancer or going to an agency all come with very different prices and levels of support.

The costs people forget

The build is only part of it. A website also needs:

  • A domain name (your .co.uk or .com address), renewed every year
  • Hosting, which keeps the site online
  • An SSL certificate, so it shows as secure
  • Changes and fixes after launch: new prices, photos, opening hours, or something that stops working

Some quotes look cheap because they leave these out. Always ask what happens after the site goes live, and what each change will cost.

Questions to ask any web designer

  • Is hosting included, and what does it cost each month or year?
  • Who owns the domain name?
  • How many changes can I make after launch, and how quickly are they done?
  • Can I update it myself from my phone?
  • Is there a minimum contract, and what happens if I leave?
  • Will it work well on phones?
  • Can I see websites you’ve built for real businesses?

What NEMORA charges

We have three fixed-price packages for the design and build, each with its own monthly plan for hosting, your domain, security and urgent fixes. Every plan has a 12-month minimum term.

  • Starter, £400 then £25 a month: a one-page website with a contact form and click-to-call. Content changes are quoted when you need them. First year: £700 in total.
  • Business, £795 then £50 a month: up to 5 pages, your own admin area to update it from your phone, an enquiries inbox and a photo gallery, plus up to 1 hour of changes every month. First year: £1,395 in total.
  • Premium, £1,600 then £70 a month: up to 10 pages, plus events or listings, booking requests and card payments through Stripe, with up to 2 hours of changes every month. First year: £2,440 in total.

Half of the setup fee is paid upfront to book your project.

Member areas, directories and marketplaces are quoted individually. See everything that’s included, or look at websites we’ve built at this price and above.
